intro: Heavy rhythmic attacks and a one-beat Presto turn a friend’s piano playing into an orchestral argument. The portrait is compact, with percussion driving its momentum.
question: What happens when rhythm matters more than a singing tune?

sections.label: VII · Presto portrait
sections.mNote: insistent rhythm displaces the theme’s hesitant character

cues.title: One large beat
cues.text: The score marks one whole-note beat to the bar and a very fast Presto. Timpani and low strings propel the opening; hear the larger rhythmic shove beneath the rapid surface activity.
cues.evidence: Novello p. 35, rehearsal 23: 1/1 metre, timpani with cellos and basses. The score identifies the forces, not the analysis’s unreliable beat estimate.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Arthur Troyte Griffith
cues.text: Arthur Troyte Griffith is a Malvern architect and a close friend of Elgar. The composer’s joke concerns his limited piano technique; it is not a claim that the orchestra is recreating a real storm.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies Griffith and the piano-playing association. The alternative storm anecdote is withheld. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 35–46, rehearsal figures 23–29. Whole-variation passage map, with measured changes at 0:12, 0:22, 0:32 and 0:38 distinguishing the main surges and lighter middle. The first state lasts only the opening seconds.

timeline.note: Timpani and low strings begin the rhythmic argument (p. 35).
Wind, upper strings and brass rapidly gather around the continuing rhythmic figure (pp. 35–36).
Running upper strings oppose emphatic wind and brass gestures in the first larger surge (pp. 38–39).
A lighter string-led passage keeps the motion going beneath restrained wind support (pp. 40–42).
The orchestral weight rebuilds around the fast string figures (pp. 42–44).
Piccolo joins the upper edge while brass gives the late phrases greater force (pp. 44–45).
Brass chords and a last string flourish bring the short portrait to its orchestral stop (p. 46).

facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
